captions.text: The reader is annoyed by her, just like her
family is, but we excuse it as harmless.
O'Connor shows us it is the opposite of harmless.
And here is where the story takes a turn
that completely upends our moral expectations.
Because if the grandmother's goodness is a sham, what
about the villain? O'Connor sets it up so that
the murderer is the only real theologian in the
book. This is undoubtedly one of the most brilliant
and unsettling inversions in all of American literature.
Let's drop back into that post-crash scene.
The family is sitting in this red gutted ditch.
A big black battered hearse-like automobile
slowly approaches and stops on the hill above them.
The Misfit steps out.
He is shirtless. He's wearing blue jeans that are
too tight for him, holding a black hat and
a gun. But the physical detail that stands out
is that his hair is just beginning to gray.
And he wears these delicate silver rim spectacles that
give him a distinctly scholarly look.
Right. He doesn't look like a monster.
No. And when he speaks, he isn't a ranting
lunatic. He's calm. He's polite.
Almost embarrassed by the situation.
He apologizes to the women for not wearing a
shirt, which is such a bizarre thing to care
about right before you murder someone.
Totally. He talks about his father.
He talks about his time in the penitentiary.
And then amidst this impending violence, he delivers this
incredible theological thesis. Jesus
thrown everything off balance.
If we connect this to the bigger picture, the
murderer is the only person in the story asking
the right questions. The Misfit's crisis is not
a performance. It is completely genuine.
He lays out a perfect terrifying theological binary
for the grandmother. He says, "If he did what
he said, then it's nothing for you to do
but throw away everything and follow him.
And if he didn't, then it's nothing for you
to do but enjoy the few minutes you got
left the best way you can by killing somebody
or burning down his house or doing some other
